title: KV cache investigation — reuse rates, eviction, paging, memory bandwidth
content:
Summary:

This doc collects results from a set of profiling and benchmark experiments focused on the KV cache subsystem in the serving runtime. The goal is to understand KV reuse rates, eviction behavior, paging to host memory, and the memory bandwidth impact under realistic LLM inference workloads. We ran microbenchmarks and end-to-end traces (LLama-2-like and Mistral-like models) to identify bottlenecks and propose mitigations.

Goals:
- Measure effective KV reuse rate (per-request and cross-request).
- Measure eviction frequency and identify causes (memory pressure, TTL, explicit eviction).
- Quantify paging behavior when KV cache exceeds GPU-resident capacity (page-in/out rates, latency).
- Measure memory bandwidth utilization attributable to KV reads/writes.
- Evaluate impact of eviction policy, cache sizing, and concurrent request patterns on latency and throughput.

Background:
Our runtime maintains per-shard KV caches for past attention key/value blobs to accelerate autoregressive decoding. Cache entries are measured by sequence prefix and request id; entries may be shared when identical prefix tokens are seen across requests. Current default policy: shard-local LRU with periodic soft-TTL, capacity configured as bytes per-GPU. Recent customer reports show tail latency spikes and throughput variability when models are served at high concurrency with large max sequence lengths.

Methodology:
- Benchmarks: a) Microbench: synthetic decode workload with controlled prefix reuse (0%, 25%, 50%, 75%, 95%), b) Service-like: batched production traces sampled from Redwood-hosted workloads (mix of short chat and long composition requests).
- Models: 13B and 70B family configs (quantized kernels) to get varied KV sizes (per-token KV size ~3.2KB for 70B).
- Hardware: A100-80GB and H100-80GB instances, 8 concurrent worker threads per GPU, batching disabled for tail-latency tests and enabled for throughput tests.
- Tools: nvprof/nsight for memory BW, perf and eBPF off-CPU traces for mutex contention, custom tracer for KV cache ops (hits, misses, evictions, page-ins), and CPU/GPU wall-clock latency histograms.
- Metrics collected: reuse_rate (% reuse of KV from cache), hit_rate, eviction_rate (evictions/sec), page_in_bytes/sec, page_out_bytes/sec, GPU memory BW (GB/s), median/p95/p99 latency.

Key findings:
1) Reuse rate vs latency:
- When reuse_rate >= 75% for a given prefix distribution, decoding latency median improves by ~28% and p99 improves by ~22% compared to cold-cache baseline.
- Reuse drops sharply with small perturbations in prefix tokenization (e.g., tokenization boundary shifts across requests) — reuse effective only when exact KV keys match.

2) Evictions and their causes:
- With default capacity=40GB per GPU, eviction_rate increased 4x under the heavy long-sequence mix on 70B. Evictions correlated strongly with peak concurrent long requests rather than aggregate token volume (spike-driven).
- Most evictions happen in bursts during request start-up (initial decode steps for long sequence), causing re-population churn and higher page-in activity.

3) Paging to host memory (GPU <-> host transfers):
- When working set exceeds GPU resident KV capacity by ~10–15%, we observe sustained page-out and page-in activity. Page-ins dominate on decode start; measured page-in bandwidth ~18 GB/s on A100 (cold pages), which adds ~18–35 ms per affected request depending on amount moved.
- Repeated eviction/paging (churn) causes tail latency amplification: p99 increased up to 2.3x vs no-paging baseline for a mixed workload.

4) Memory bandwidth and contention:
- KV reads during attention consume significant device memory bandwidth. In high-reuse scenarios, reads are bursty but confined to cached portions; measured sustained memory BW attributable to KV reads was ~210 GB/s on H100 in peak decode windows (out of ~900 GB/s device peak).
- Kernel-level profiling shows that when page-in is active, PCIe/NVLink link bandwidth becomes a bottleneck; GPU compute stalls waiting for KV page data, increasing decode latency.

5) Concurrency and lock contention:
- eBPF traces show per-shard cache locks experience contention at >= 12 concurrent requests, adding ~3–7 ms per cache op under lock hold times of 1–2 ms. Contention aggravates eviction decisions under bursts.

Experiments and configurations tested:
- Baseline: LRU, capacity 40GB, soft-TTL=10min.
- LRU vs Segmented LRU (windowed LFU + LRU): Segmented reduced eviction churn by ~18% for workloads with a small hot set (10% of keys), improving p99 by ~9%.
- Resident-overprovisioning: +10% reserved headroom (capacity 44GB) eliminated sustained paging in most traces and reduced p99 by ~14% for the worst-case mix, at cost of reduced multi-tenant density.
- Prefetching heuristic: prefetch first N tokens of an incoming request's KV into GPU (based on length estimate) — reduced cold-start page-ins by ~40% and p95 latency by 12% for long requests.
- Lockless read path for hot entries: implementing versioned read (read-copy) for hot bucket reduced lock contention metrics and improved median cache op latency by 2–5 ms.

Representative numbers (70B model, mixed workload, H100):
- Cold baseline median decode latency (first 128 tokens): 95 ms
- High-reuse scenario median: 68 ms
- Eviction-churn scenario p99: 430 ms
- With segmented LRU + headroom: p99 reduced to 315 ms

Observations and interpretations:
- Exact-match semantics for KV keys makes reuse brittle to small tokenization changes. We should explore normalized-key hashing or prefix-canonicalization to improve cross-request reuse.
- Evictions are bursty and driven by request concurrency spikes. Static capacity allocation is fragile under bursty workloads; a combination of predictable admission control and transient headroom helps.
- Paging is expensive: even though NVLink/PCIe link can move tens of GB/s, latency of page-in (stalling compute) hurts tail latency. Avoiding paging by keeping a conservative headroom per GPU is the most straightforward mitigation.
- Lock contention suggests shard-level locking is a scalability limiter; lockless or finer-grained locks plus hot-path optimizations matter for p99.

Recommendations (short term):
1) Increase default per-GPU KV headroom by +10% for long-sequence model profiles (configurable per-model).
2) Add an optional segmented-LRU eviction policy accessible via model config.
3) Implement a prefetch-on-admission heuristic: when a long request is admitted, prefetch first K tokens into GPU memory before scheduling heavy GPU compute.
4) Prototype a lockless fast-path for hot KV reads (versioned read) to reduce contention under high concurrency.
5) Provide a runtime flag to prioritize low-latency requests (pin headroom) vs throughput-oriented requests (best-effort eviction).

Recommendations (medium term / research):
- Explore approximate-key reuse matching (fuzzy keying) to increase reuse across tokenization jitter — careful evaluation needed to avoid correctness regressions.
- Investigate a distributed cache directory to enable cross-GPU sharing of hot KV entries without full duplication.
- Evaluate adaptive capacity sizing driven by recent request concurrency and working-set estimation (auto-headroom).

Next steps / Action items:
- PR: implement segmented LRU toggle and prefetch heuristic (owner: Priya) — linked PR https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/412 (INF-2431)
- Spike: prototype lockless read fast-path and measure p99 delta (owner: Ethan) — 2 week spike.
- Add detailed telemetry: per-request KV size, per-shard page-in/out counters surfaced in Console (owner: Sofia).
- Run extended soak on staging with mixed real traces for 72 hours after changes to validate multi-tenant impact.

Open questions / risks:
- How much customer-side changes (prompt normalization) are feasible to improve reuse?
- Trade-offs between multi-tenant density and latency when increasing headroom — need business input on acceptable capacity loss.
- Potential correctness/performance risk of fuzzy-keying; will require canarying and evals.

Appendix: quick experiment table (sample):

| Config | Reuse | Evictions/sec | Page-in GB/s | p99 latency (ms) | Notes |
|--------|-------:|--------------:|-------------:|-----------------:|-------|
| Baseline LRU (40GB) | 42% | 18 | 12 | 430 | heavy churn, paging |
| SegLRU (40GB) | 47% | 14 | 11 | 392 | better hot retention |
| Baseline +10% headroom | 39% | 6 | 1.8 | 315 | paging avoided |
| Prefetch enabled | 41% | 12 | 7 | 378 | reduced cold-start cost |

Notes on reproducibility:
- Bench harness, trace snippets, and run scripts are checked into serving-runtime repo under /bench/kv-cache (see PR above). Use the provided trace-replayer to reproduce microbench and service-like mixes.

If reviewers want raw traces and tracer logs for the runs above, I can upload a subset to Google Drive (large files) and share links.

-- Jordan
